activities.anchor: move along the prices and compare the two series
activities.caption: mark the price where the market clears
activities.name: sdEquilPlace

config.prompt: At £30 buyers want 40 units and sellers offer 40. At £20 there is a shortage; at £50 a surplus. Place the equilibrium price.
config.why: Only at £30 do the quantities match at 40. Below it, the shortage bids the price up; above it, the surplus forces it down.

activities.anchor: The exam's favourite trap lives here
activities.caption: movement along the curve, or a shift?
activities.name: sdMoveSort

config.prompt: File each event: does it move you along the demand curve, or shift the whole curve?

items.label: coffee's price falls, so buyers order more
incomes rise, so restaurant meals are in greater demand
a health study makes tea more popular
the price of tea rises, so less tea is bought
the population grows, so more housing is wanted
a sale cuts the price, so more jumpers sell

config.why: A price change moves you along a fixed curve; incomes, tastes, substitutes and population shift the whole curve.

activities.anchor: Sellers offer more at higher prices because producing more tends to cost more
activities.caption: pair each event with its supply shift
activities.name: sdSupplyMatch

config.prompt: Pair each event with the supply shift it causes:

pairs.left: a better picking machine is invented

config.why: Input costs, technology, taxes and subsidies shift supply; a price change would only move along the curve.

activities.anchor: Put the curves together and equilibrium does the coordinating
activities.caption: a shortage becomes an equilibrium
activities.name: sdAdjustOrder

config.prompt: A shortage becomes an equilibrium — put the adjustment in order:
items: At £20, buyers demand 60 units but sellers offer only 20
A shortage of 40 appears, and frustrated buyers bid the price up
As the price rises, quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises
At £30 the two quantities meet at 40
The shortage disappears and the price stops moving
config.why: The price is the adjustment mechanism: a shortage pulls it up, a surplus pushes it down, and the crossing is where the pressure ends.

activities.anchor: the outcomes must be argued case by case
activities.caption: two curves move at once — what is certain?
activities.name: sdDoubleBranch

config.root: A fashion trend shifts demand right at the same time as a better machine shifts supply right. What can you say for certain?

start.text: Both curves have moved. Which outcome is unambiguous?

choices.label: Quantity rises; the price change is ambiguous
choices.feedback: Yes — both shifts raise quantity, but they pull price in opposite directions.

choices.label: Price rises and quantity falls
choices.feedback: Check the directions: both changes raise quantity.

choices.label: Price certainly rises
choices.feedback: Demand pushes price up, but the supply shift pushes it down.

qty.text: Quantity rises for sure. Demand up raises price, supply up lowers it, so the net price depends on which shift is larger.

wrong1.text: That gets both directions wrong: demand up and supply up both raise quantity.

choices.label: So what is certain?
choices.feedback: Only the quantity direction is guaranteed.

wrong2.text: Price is the ambiguous part — the two shifts pull it in opposite directions.

choices.label: Then what can I say?
choices.feedback: Quantity rises, price depends on the sizes.

config.why: With both curves shifting, argue which shift dominates; here only the quantity direction is guaranteed.

activities.anchor: Two markets can react to the same price rise with completely different rage
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the elasticity formula
activities.name: sdPedCloze

config.text: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in %%0%% divided by the percentage change in %%1%%. At −0.5, demand is %%2%%, so a price rise will %%3%% total revenue.
config.hint: Elasticity compares quantity's percentage response with price's percentage change; below 1 in magnitude is inelastic.

activities.anchor: asks the same question of sellers
activities.caption: call the supply elasticity
activities.name: sdPesEst

config.prompt: A 20% rise in coffee's price raises the quantity supplied by 10%. What is the price elasticity of supply?
config.why: PES = 10% ÷ 20% = 0.5 — inelastic. Coffee trees take years to bear, so growers cannot respond quickly.
config.context: manufacturing with spare capacity is far more elastic

activities.anchor: is the claim that this price mechanism
activities.caption: true or false — where markets fail
activities.name: sdFailureJudge

statements.s: A factory's smoke that harms neighbours is a negative externality the market price does not include.
statements.why: The neighbours never bargained, so the cost lands outside the transaction.

statements.s: Street lighting is a public good because it is non-excludable and non-rival.
statements.why: One person's use does not diminish another's, and non-payers cannot be excluded — so private markets under-provide it.

statements.s: A monopoly prices at the competitive equilibrium.
statements.why: A monopolist restricts quantity and raises price above marginal cost, away from the competitive crossing.

activities.anchor: The formula is easiest with honest numbers
activities.caption: find the elasticity slip
activities.name: sdCafeSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the café's elasticity reasoning goes wrong:
lines: A café raises its price from £3.00 to £3.30, a 10% increase.
Sales fall from 100 cups to 85, a 15% decrease.
Since |PED| > 1, demand is inelastic, so the price rise should raise revenue.
But revenue actually falls from £300 to £280.50.
config.correction: |PED| > 1 means elastic, not inelastic — and elastic demand is exactly why the price rise lost money.
config.why: The revenue check confirms the classification: £300 → £280.50 means the quantity effect dominated.

activities.caption: two triangles, one market — drag the divider
activities.name: sdSurplusCompare

config.prompt: Two triangles in one market — drag the divider:

before.label: consumer surplus
before.text: buyers who would have paid more than the equilibrium price keep the gap — value received but not paid for

after.label: producer surplus
after.text: sellers who would have supplied below the equilibrium price keep the gap — payment received above their cost

config.why: The two triangles together measure the value the market creates; competition maximises their sum, while taxes, monopoly and price controls shrink it.
